body.en: Git stores snapshots of files in **commits**; **branches** are movable pointers to commits; you integrate work with **merges** (or rebases); on GitHub, changes are proposed through **pull requests (PRs)** where reviewers comment and automated checks (CI) run. For databases, the SQL project's `.sql` files ARE the source — every table, view and procedure has a file that goes through the same review flow as application code.

heading.en: Configuring source control for SQL projects

body.en:
- Commit the `.sqlproj`, all object `.sql` files, pre/post-deployment scripts, publish profiles (without secrets) and the `.refactorlog`.
- Ignore build output: `bin/`, `obj/` (the .dacpac is a CI artifact).
- One object per file, folders by schema/object type — clean diffs and easy reviews.
- **SQL database in Fabric** has built-in Git integration (Azure DevOps or GitHub) that syncs the database as an SDK-style project; Azure SQL/SQL Server use the VS Code extension or `Extract` to create the project, then normal Git.
- Keep app code and database project in the same repo when they release together (atomic PRs), or separate repos with versioned dacpac packages when teams/cadences differ.

sections.code:
# .gitignore for a SQL project
bin/
obj/
*.dbmdl
*.user
*.publish.xml.user

body.en:
Common strategy: **trunk-based / GitHub flow** — short-lived feature branches off `main`, PR back to `main`, CI validates, merge, deploy. Larger teams may add release branches. Database-specific guidance:
- Keep branches short-lived: long-lived schema branches drift and produce painful conflicts.
- PRs should show both the object diff AND, ideally, the generated deployment script (SqlPackage Script/DeployReport) as a CI artifact or comment, so reviewers see the real ALTERs (e.g. a table rebuild!).
- CI on every PR: build the project (validation), run unit tests, optionally deploy to an ephemeral database.
- Use **expand/contract** changes so schema and app can deploy independently.

Because each object is one declarative file, conflicts are usually localized: two developers changing the same procedure → resolve like any code conflict, then **rebuild** — the build is your safety net (a merged view may now reference a column the other branch removed). SDK-style globbing removes the classic `.sqlproj` file-list conflicts. Watch for semantic conflicts that merge cleanly but break: e.g., branch A renames a column (refactorlog), branch B adds a view using the old name — only the build/tests catch it. Re-run CI after resolving and before merging.

Never commit secrets (connection strings with passwords, API keys) — not in publish profiles, appsettings, or scripts. Options, best first:
- **No secret at all**: workflows authenticate to Azure with **OpenID Connect (OIDC) federated credentials** (`azure/login` with client-id/tenant-id/subscription-id, no client secret); the database uses **Entra authentication** for the deployment identity.
- **GitHub Actions secrets**, scoped at repository, organization or **environment** level (environment secrets are only available to jobs targeting that environment, after its protection rules pass).
- **Azure Key Vault** for app/runtime secrets, read via managed identity.
Also: enable **secret scanning / push protection** in GitHub to block accidental commits; rotate any secret that ever reached Git history (deleting the line doesn't remove it from history).

sections.code:
permissions:
  id-token: write      # required for OIDC
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    environment: production       # environment secrets + protection rules
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

examTips.en: Commit .sqlproj, .sql, pre/post scripts, profiles (no secrets) and .refactorlog; ignore bin/obj — the dacpac is a CI artifact.
Short-lived branches + PRs with CI (build, tests, generated deploy script) is the expected workflow.
After resolving conflicts, rebuild: clean text merges can still break references (semantic conflicts).
OIDC federated credentials = no stored Azure secret in GitHub; requires permissions: id-token: write.
Environment secrets are only exposed to jobs that reference that environment (and pass its protection rules).
A secret pushed to Git must be rotated — removing it in a later commit doesn't erase history.
Fabric SQL database supports Git integration that stores the DB as an SDK-style project.
